title: Chintan Pandya, Roni Mazumdar and Vijay Kumar Won't Apologize for Indian Food
excerpt: The Unapologetic Foods founders and Semma's chef-partner built America's most decorated Indian restaurant group by refusing to dilute regional cooking.
body:
• Unapologetic Foods founders Chintan Pandya and Roni Mazumdar built Adda, Dhamaka and Semma on a refusal to dilute regional Indian cooking for American palates.
  • Semma, led by chef-partner Vijay Kumar, topped The New York Times list of the best restaurants in New York for 2025, and Kumar won the James Beard Award for Best Chef: New York State in 2025, after Pandya's win in 2022.
  • The group now runs eight concepts in New York, seven of them Indian, and is opening its first restaurant outside the city, a second Adda in Philadelphia.
  • Its model hands the spotlight to other chefs — Kumar at Semma, Eric Valdez at the Filipino concept Naks — rather than building around a single name.

Three of the most decorated figures in American Indian cooking share a founding refusal: the food will not be softened, sweetened or explained away for American diners. Chef Chintan Pandya and restaurateur Roni Mazumdar built that refusal into the name of their group, Unapologetic Foods, and chef-partner Vijay Kumar has carried it to its highest honors at Semma, the Tamil restaurant in New York's West Village.

Two immigrants, one argument

Pandya and Mazumdar met through a mutual friend, according to Fine Dining Lovers, and opened their first collaboration, Rahi, in 2017. It went largely unnoticed. Mazumdar came to the United States from Kolkata as a middle school student; his father, a lawyer in India, sold fruit from a cart in New York before becoming a traffic cop, and later ran the Lower East Side spot Masalawala, where his son helped. Pandya emigrated from Mumbai in his 30s after cooking at hotels in Singapore and at Junoon, the Michelin-starred Indian restaurant in New York.

Their shared complaint was that Indian food in America had been compressed into a generic menu no Indian would choose at home, while regional cooking — the food of villages, homes and specific states — had no commercial stage. Pandya put the principle bluntly to Platform Magazine:

"There's only one crime — when you never actually express it in its own real format."

— Chintan Pandya, Chef and Partner, Unapologetic Foods

Adda, Dhamaka, Semma

Adda Indian Canteen, opened in Long Island City a year after Rahi, tested the thesis with dishes such as goat brains alongside the best possible versions of familiar plates. Dhamaka, on the Lower East Side, went further into the regional cooking Pandya had collected on travels through rural India: Champaran meat from Bihar, cooked in clay pots — Platform counted 25 pots a day, each needing more than a day of preparation — alongside dishes from Meghalaya, Odisha and Rajasthan that rarely appear on American menus.

Semma completed the arc. Kumar, who grew up in Tamil Nadu, was given carte blanche over its menu, in Platform's account, and cooked the food of his home state without translation. Semma received its first Michelin star in the fall of 2022, when it stood as the only Indian restaurant in the United States holding one, according to Forbes' interview with the founders. In 2025 it took the No. 1 spot on The New York Times list of the best restaurants in New York, and Kumar won the James Beard Award for Best Chef: New York State, following Pandya's own win in 2022.

Giving away the spotlight

The group's most unusual choice is structural. "It's not about us. It's about giving voice to our community," Mazumdar told Platform, describing a conscious decision not to build around a single chef. Kumar's authority at Semma is the proof, and the pattern repeated in 2024 when the group opened Naks, its first non-Indian restaurant — a Filipino concept led by Eric Valdez, who had started under Pandya as a line cook.

"One of our missions is, how do we tell our story without compromise?"

— Roni Mazumdar, Co-founder, Unapologetic Foods

Why it resonates with the diaspora

For Indian Americans, the argument lands personally. Mazumdar has recalled his school years in New York, when he hid behind pizza and sandwiches rather than the food of home. As an adult he concluded that an entire subcontinent could not be shoved into one menu. Unapologetic Foods treats regional specificity — Tamil, Bengali, Bihari — as the point rather than a risk, and the waitlists and awards suggest American diners were readier for that food than the industry assumed. Pandya describes the rooms themselves the same way: "We are not fine dining, we are fun dining."

What's next

The group is opening a second Adda in Philadelphia, its first restaurant outside New York, with more cities possible. Whether the model travels will test the founders' claim that philosophy, filtered through a local chef and neighborhood, matters more than a repeatable formula. The refusal to apologize is not a niche position anymore. It sits at the center of American Indian dining.
